narration.text: Here is a ruler held out at one end, with a weight resting on it.
Your hand is the grip on the left. The weight can slide along the ruler.
The weight tries to turn the ruler around your hand.
It is like a door turning on its hinges.
To keep the ruler level, your hand twists back just as hard.
Which is harder to hold out: the weight close to you, or far from you?
Got it. Let's test your guess.
Watch the effort gauge as the weight slides away from your hand.
The farther the weight is from your grip, the more it twists the ruler around your hand, so your hand has to push back harder.
At the far end it takes about {{effort_far_vs_near}} times the effort of the near position.

feedback.correct: You predicted far is harder, and that is what happened.
feedback.incorrect: You expected close to be harder. It is the other way round, and here is why.
feedback.unsure: You weren't sure, and that's a fair place to start. Here is what happened: far from you is harder.

explanation.title: Distance from the grip changes the effort
explanation.body: A weight twists the ruler around your hand. The twist is the weight multiplied by its distance from your hand, so the same weight twists harder the farther out it sits.
assumptions: The ruler is held still and level
The ruler is rigid and the same all along
The weight is small enough to treat as a point
limits: Says nothing about how long you can hold it or how tired your arm gets

narration.text: A robot arm works the same way.
The servo is your hand, the arm is the ruler, and the end weight is the weight.
Where the comparison breaks down: a servo does not tire like a hand; its limit comes from its motor and gears.

explanation.title: Same idea, robot arm
explanation.body: The servo has to resist the twist from the arm and the end weight, including the arm's own weight. Moving weight farther from the servo makes that twist bigger.
limits: This picture is a placeholder, not a real servo or a real arm

narration.text: If the end weight moved closer to the servo, would holding the arm level get harder or easier for the servo?

feedback.correct: Yes: closer to the servo means a shorter distance, so less twist to resist.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite: closer to the servo means a shorter distance, so less twist to resist, which is easier.
feedback.unsure: That's fine. Closer to the servo means a shorter distance, so less twist to resist, which is easier.
